summary: Documents extensions to RADIUS, already in use in network access server products, that let a server change a user's session while it runs. This includes disconnecting users and changing their authorizations. It replaces RFC 3576. It is informational because it describes deployed behavior rather than a standards-track design.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally a guard checks you once at the door. This lets the guard later say, you must leave now, or you can now go to a different room.

subtitle: How a RADIUS server can reach out to a network access server to disconnect a user or change their authorization mid-session.

tldr.problem: RADIUS does not support unsolicited messages from the server to the Network Access Server (NAS), yet administrators need to end sessions or change what a user is allowed to do while the session is running.
tldr.mechanism: Disconnect-Request and CoA-Request packets are sent by a Dynamic Authorization Client to UDP port 3799, name the NAS and session through identification attributes, and are answered with an ACK or NAK.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents what vendors had already deployed, and is Informational because known security and ambiguity problems could not be fixed without breaking those deployments. It obsoletes RFC 3576 and is updated by RFC 8559 and RFC 9765.

today: RFC 5176 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 3576. It is updated by RFC 8559 and RFC 9765.

sections.title: Why Dynamic Authorization
sections.content:
RADIUS, as defined in RFC 2865, has no way for the server to send an unsolicited message to the Network Access Server (NAS), the device that provides network access. But administrators sometimes need to terminate a user session in progress, or add and remove authorization attributes when a user's authorization level changes.

Several vendors added commands for this. Disconnect packets end sessions immediately. Change-of-Authorization (CoA) packets modify session authorization attributes such as data filters.

The RFC defines three roles. The Dynamic Authorization Client (DAC) originates the requests. The Dynamic Authorization Server (DAS) receives them, and may be a NAS or a RADIUS proxy. A session is each service the NAS provides to a user.

This is an Informational RFC, not Standards Track, because of problems that cannot be fixed without breaking deployed implementations: security weaknesses and semantic ambiguity in CoA. Fixes are recommended but cannot be mandatory.
sections.plainLanguage: Usually the door guard only talks when you arrive. This adds a phone line so the boss can call the guard later and say, send this person home, or change what this person can do.

sections.title: Disconnect and CoA Messages
sections.content:
A Disconnect-Request asks the NAS to terminate user sessions and discard all associated session context. The NAS answers with Disconnect-ACK if the sessions are gone, or Disconnect-NAK if it could not disconnect one or more. A Disconnect-ACK may carry Acct-Terminate-Cause (49) with value 6 (Admin-Reset).

A CoA-Request changes session authorizations, typically data filters. It may carry Filter-ID (11) or NAS-Filter-Rule (92). The NAS answers CoA-ACK on success or CoA-NAK otherwise. Changes are atomic: if the request fails for any matching session, the NAS MUST send a NAK and make no changes to any of them.

All attributes in these requests are treated as mandatory. A NAS MUST NAK a request with unsupported attributes or values, optionally with Error-Cause 401 (Unsupported Attribute) or 407 (Invalid Attribute Value). A Disconnect-Request MUST contain only NAS and session identification attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of calls. One says, you have to leave right now. The other says, you can still stay but here are your new rules. The guard answers yes or no, and if any part can't be done, nothing changes.

sections.title: Packet Format and Authentication
sections.content:
Requests go to UDP port 3799, and responses reverse the ports. Exactly one RADIUS packet is carried in the UDP data. The fields are Code, Identifier, Length, Authenticator and Attributes in type-length-value form, with the same meaning as in RADIUS.

The new Code values are 40 to 45 (Disconnect-Request, -ACK, -NAK and CoA-Request, -ACK, -NAK). The Length field has a minimum of 20 and a maximum of 4096. A server MUST be able to detect a duplicate request that has the same source IP address, source UDP port and Identifier within a short span of time. The client handles retransmission and MUST keep the Identifier unchanged for identical retransmissions.

The 16-octet Request Authenticator is an MD5 checksum computed the same way as for an Accounting-Request in RFC 2866. The Response Authenticator is an MD5 hash over the response Code, Identifier, Length, the Request Authenticator, the response attributes, and then the shared secret. The server MUST pick the shared secret by the source IP address of the packet.

An optional Message-Authenticator (80) attribute, calculated with HMAC-MD5 (see RFC 2104), can also protect these packets against spoofing.
sections.plainLanguage: Each call has a label with a type, a number so replies match, a length, and a secret check code made from a password only the two sides know, so a stranger cannot fake the call.

sections.title: Finding the Right Session
sections.content:
Requests identify the NAS and the sessions with attributes. NAS identification uses NAS-IP-Address (4), NAS-Identifier (32) or NAS-IPv6-Address (95). Session identification uses attributes such as User-Name (1), Acct-Session-Id (44), Framed-IP-Address (8), Calling-Station-Id (31) and others in the RFC's table. The combination MUST match at least one session, otherwise the NAS sends a NAK. If several sessions match, the request applies to all of them.

Either User-Name or Chargeable-User-Identity SHOULD be present, and an Acct-Session-Id SHOULD be included. A NAS SHOULD send an Acct-Session-Id or Acct-Multi-Session-Id in its Access-Request so the client can learn it.

A CoA-Request can include Service-Type Authorize Only plus a State attribute. The NAS then replies with a CoA-NAK carrying Error-Cause 507 (Request Initiated), and sends its own Access-Request to the RADIUS server, which answers with Access-Accept or Access-Reject. This helps translate to Diameter, and is how a change like renumbering can be done, since address attributes serve as identifiers in CoA-Request.

Proxies must pass Proxy-State attributes through as opaque data, may add at most one, and must remove their own from the response and recompute the response integrity check.
sections.plainLanguage: To send someone home, the boss must say which building and which person. If the description fits several people, all of them are affected.

sections.title: Error-Cause Codes
sections.content:
The Error-Cause attribute (type 101, length 6) explains why a NAK was sent. Values 200 to 299 mean success and appear only in ACKs. Values 400 to 499 are fatal errors by the client, and 500 to 599 are fatal errors on the server side. Both may appear in NAKs.

Examples include 401 Unsupported Attribute, 402 Missing Attribute, 403 NAS Identification Mismatch, 503 Session Context Not Found and 508 Multiple Session Selection Unsupported. This RFC allocates the values 407 (Invalid Attribute Value) and 508 in the IANA registry. The RFC also gives suggested mappings from these values to Diameter Result-Code values.
sections.plainLanguage: When the guard says no, he also gives a reason code, like 'wrong person' or 'could not find them'. The numbers tell the boss whose mistake it was.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Where one NAS is shared by several providers, one provider must not be able to disconnect or change another's users. A server MUST silently discard requests from untrusted sources. A proxy MAY apply a reverse path forwarding (RPF) check: use the session identification attributes to find the RADIUS servers that an equivalent Access-Request could be routed to, and discard the request if its source is not among them. Servers SHOULD use a different shared secret for each client.

Existing implementations rely on MD5-based authentication with known weaknesses, so the RFC RECOMMENDS IPsec, with a policy such as requiring IPsec to destination port UDP 3799.

Existing implementations lack replay protection. Where IPsec replay protection is not used, an Event-Timestamp (55) attribute SHOULD be included, and packets that are not current within a time window MUST be silently discarded. The RFC says a default window of 300 seconds should be adequate in many circumstances.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the right boss may phone the guard. The guard should check that a call really came from an allowed office, use a stronger lock than the old one, and ignore an old call someone is replaying.
